title: Computational Fluid Dynamics
tagline: Governing equations, finite differences and finite volumes, stability, convection schemes, linear solvers, pressure–velocity coupling, turbulence modelling, and verification and validation
summary: Computational fluid dynamics solves the equations of fluid flow and heat transfer numerically and is now part of almost every thermofluids design. The course covers the conservation equations and their mathematical character, finite-difference and finite-volume discretisation, consistency, stability and convergence, schemes for diffusion and convection, the solution of the discrete equations, pressure–velocity coupling for incompressible flow, turbulence modelling, meshing and boundary conditions, and the verification and validation of results.
overview: Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solves the conservation equations of mass, momentum and energy numerically, on a mesh of small cells covering the flow domain. Where analytical fluid mechanics is confined to simple geometries and idealised flows, CFD handles the complex shapes, turbulence and heat transfer of real devices — pumps, heat exchangers, wings, combustors, ventilation systems — and is now used routinely throughout thermofluids design. It is also easy to misuse: a CFD code always produces an answer, and the answer always looks plausible.

This course builds the method from the ground up, in the order in which a general-purpose code is constructed. It starts from the governing equations in integral and differential form and their classification as elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic, which decides how a problem can be solved and what boundary conditions it needs. Finite differences introduce truncation error and order of accuracy; von Neumann analysis, the CFL condition and the Lax equivalence theorem explain stability and convergence; and the finite volume method, which conserves exactly on any mesh, is developed first for diffusion and then for convection, where the competition between accuracy and boundedness leads to upwind, QUICK and TVD schemes.

The second half addresses what makes practical CFD demanding: solving systems with millions of unknowns efficiently (iterative methods, multigrid and Krylov solvers), coupling pressure and velocity in incompressible flow (staggered grids, Rhie–Chow interpolation, SIMPLE, PISO and projection methods), and representing turbulence through Reynolds averaging, eddy-viscosity models such as $k$–$\varepsilon$ and $k$–$\omega$ SST, wall treatment and large-eddy simulation. The final lesson covers meshes, boundary conditions and the verification and validation procedures — manufactured solutions, Richardson extrapolation, the grid convergence index and the ASME V&V 20 comparison — that turn a simulation into an engineering result with a stated uncertainty.

The course assumes fluid mechanics, heat transfer and the numerical analysis of a first course (Taylor series, linear systems, ODE integrators). Every lesson works through small problems by hand — five-cell conduction and convection problems, a single pressure correction, a three-grid convergence study — because the behaviour of a large code is best understood on a problem small enough to check with a calculator.
outcomes: Derive the integral and differential conservation equations of fluid flow and classify model equations as elliptic, parabolic or hyperbolic, stating the boundary data each type requires.
Construct finite-difference approximations by Taylor series and determine their truncation error, order of accuracy and modified wavenumber.
Analyse the stability of explicit and implicit schemes by von Neumann analysis and the CFL condition, and explain convergence through the Lax equivalence theorem.
Discretise steady and unsteady diffusion problems by the finite volume method, including boundary conditions, interface conductivities and source linearisation.
Select a convection scheme (central, upwind, hybrid, QUICK or a TVD limiter) from the cell Péclet number and the need for boundedness, and estimate the numerical diffusion it introduces.

Solve the discrete equations with direct and iterative methods, estimate their convergence rate from the spectral radius, and explain why multigrid and preconditioned Krylov methods are used for large problems.
Explain pressure–velocity decoupling and derive the SIMPLE pressure-correction equation, Rhie–Chow interpolation and the projection method.
Choose a turbulence model and near-wall mesh for a given flow, and estimate first-cell heights and inlet turbulence quantities.
Carry out a grid-convergence study with Richardson extrapolation and the grid convergence index, and compare simulation with experiment using a validation uncertainty.

chapters.title: Governing equations and their classification
chapters.summary: The conservation laws in integral and differential form, and elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic behaviour.

chapters.title: Finite differences
chapters.summary: Taylor-series approximations of derivatives, truncation error, and explicit and implicit schemes for model equations.

chapters.title: Consistency, stability and convergence
chapters.summary: Von Neumann stability analysis, the CFL condition, numerical diffusion and dispersion, and the Lax equivalence theorem.

chapters.title: The finite volume method for diffusion
chapters.summary: Control-volume discretisation of steady and unsteady diffusion problems, with heat-conduction examples.

chapters.title: Solving the discrete equations
chapters.summary: Direct and iterative solvers, multigrid acceleration, and monitoring convergence.

chapters.title: Convection–diffusion schemes
chapters.summary: Central, upwind and higher-order schemes, the Péclet number, boundedness and flux limiters.

chapters.title: Pressure–velocity coupling
chapters.summary: Staggered and collocated grids, the SIMPLE family of algorithms and fractional-step methods for incompressible flow.

chapters.title: Turbulence modelling
chapters.summary: Reynolds averaging, eddy-viscosity models such as k–ε and k–ω SST, wall treatment, and large-eddy simulation.

chapters.title: Meshing, boundary conditions and verification
chapters.summary: Structured and unstructured meshes, boundary conditions, grid-convergence studies, and verification and validation.

history.title: Finite differences for a masonry dam
history.detail: Lewis Fry Richardson computes the stresses in a masonry dam by finite differences in the *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A*, the first systematic numerical solution of a PDE problem, and proposes extrapolating results from two grids.

history.title: The CFL condition
history.detail: Courant, Friedrichs and Lewy publish their analysis of difference equations in *Mathematische Annalen*, showing that the numerical domain of dependence must contain the physical one.

history.title: Flow past a cylinder computed by hand
history.detail: Alexander Thom publishes a numerical solution of the steady viscous flow past a circular cylinder at low Reynolds number in the *Proceedings of the Royal Society A*, usually regarded as the first numerical solution of the Navier–Stokes equations for flow past a body.

history.title: The Lax equivalence theorem
history.detail: Peter Lax and Robert Richtmyer prove that a consistent linear scheme for a well-posed problem converges if and only if it is stable.

history.title: The staggered-grid MAC method
history.detail: Harlow and Welch of Los Alamos publish the Marker-and-Cell method in *Physics of Fluids*, introducing the staggered grid for incompressible flow with a free surface.

history.title: The SIMPLE algorithm
history.detail: Patankar and Spalding publish the SIMPLE pressure-correction procedure in the *International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer*; it becomes the basis of most industrial finite-volume codes.

history.title: The k–ε turbulence model
history.detail: Jones and Launder publish the two-equation k–ε model in the *International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer*; with the constants of Launder and Sharma (1974) it becomes the standard engineering turbulence model.

history.title: Rhie–Chow interpolation
history.detail: Rhie and Chow's momentum interpolation, published in the *AIAA Journal*, suppresses pressure checkerboarding on collocated grids and opens the way to unstructured finite-volume codes.

history.title: SST model and grid convergence index
history.detail: Florian Menter publishes the k–ω SST turbulence model in the *AIAA Journal*, and Patrick Roache proposes the grid convergence index for reporting mesh-refinement studies in the *Journal of Fluids Engineering*.

history.title: ASME V&V 20
history.detail: ASME publishes V&V 20, the *Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Fluid Dynamics and Heat Transfer*, defining the comparison error and validation uncertainty.

references.title: An Introduction to Computational Fluid Dynamics: The Finite Volume Method
references.authors: H. K. Versteeg and W. Malalasekera
references.note: 2nd edition (Pearson). The most accessible introduction to the finite volume method, with worked 1D examples of diffusion, convection schemes and SIMPLE that parallel this course.

references.title: Computational Methods for Fluid Dynamics
references.authors: J. H. Ferziger, M. Perić and R. L. Street
references.note: 4th edition (Springer). Rigorous coverage of discretisation, solvers, pressure–velocity coupling, complex geometries and error estimation; the standard graduate text.

references.title: Numerical Heat Transfer and Fluid Flow
references.note: Hemisphere/McGraw-Hill. The original exposition of the control-volume method, the four basic rules and SIMPLE; short and still very readable.

references.title: Finite Volume Methods for Hyperbolic Problems
references.note: Cambridge University Press. Conservation laws, upwinding, Godunov's theorem, TVD schemes and limiters treated carefully.

references.title: Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems
references.note: 2nd edition (SIAM). Splitting methods, Krylov solvers and preconditioning for the large sparse systems of CFD.

references.title: Turbulent Flows
references.note: Cambridge University Press. Reynolds averaging, the law of the wall, turbulence models and large-eddy simulation from first principles.

references.title: Turbulence Modeling for CFD
references.note: 3rd edition (DCW Industries). The practitioner's guide to RANS models, their derivation, calibration and limitations.

references.title: Verification and Validation in Computational Science and Engineering
references.note: Hermosa Publishers. The source of the grid convergence index and of systematic code and solution verification, including manufactured solutions.
